Three findings weaken the original expectation:

- Moving the contour preserves contributions that can reappear on connecting faces and spatial complements.
- With the same holomorphic approximation and correlated uncertainty, the two paths give exactly the same estimate. Basic absolute-error bounds can become worse along the longer path.
- Positivity of the real relative energy does not survive automatically in the complete complex-time integral.

There is still a legitimate possibility: **negative-time smoothing might make the actual theta calculation substantially easier or cheaper**, even though the complete integral is constrained by the boundary identity. Equality of exact quantities does not prevent one representation from being easier to estimate. We have not tested that possibility with actual theta data.

My recommendation is to give this **at most one small feasibility comparison**, requiring a clear improvement in the complete bound or total verification cost before extending it. Without that improvement, I would set this mechanism aside. More contour identities alone are unlikely to change the assessment.

The connection checks out with a useful uniform bound: under RH, the number of zero labels belonging to multiple zeros at time zero is at most three times the number of pair-matrix eigenvalues above \(1/(4t)\) at positive time \(t\).

This gives us a concrete target smaller than full PCC: prove that the proportion of eigenvalues above that threshold tends to zero at a suitable height-dependent time. I’m saving the derivation and updating the research plan. The spectral upper bound itself remains unproved.

Yes—I found the [earlier pair-matrix work](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/11_late_heat_caps_and_charge_transport/notes/06_PAIR_DISTANCE_MATRICES_AND_FORCED_HEAT_DISSIPATION_20261022.md), and it gives a concrete route toward your almost-all simplicity target.

The useful spectral object is the inverse-square gap matrix \(L\), related to the squared Vandermonde by
\[
\Delta=\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)^2,
\qquad L=\tfrac12\nabla^2(-\log\Delta).
\]
An \(m\)-fold zero at time zero produces \(m-1\) eigenvalues growing like \(1/t\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Thus multiplicities leave a detectable signature in the spectrum.

More usefully, combining the earlier complete gap-evolution equation with a matrix comparison gives this **uniform implication under RH**:
\[
\boxed{
M_0\le 3\,\#\{\lambda(L(t))\ge 1/(4t)\}.
}
\]
Here \(M_0\) counts zero labels belonging to multiple endpoint zeros, and the finite population includes complete endpoint clusters and their tracked descendants.

**Therefore, almost-all simplicity would follow if we could show that these large eigenvalues occupy a vanishing fraction of the spectrum at a suitable height-dependent time.** Full PCC would be stronger than necessary. I also derived a bounded spectral statistic that suffices and is less sensitive to isolated extremely small gaps.

The missing step is an independent theta estimate for that spectral distribution. The earlier work supplies the evolution equations, but its late-time clock estimates do not cover the required regime near time zero. And yes: RH implying almost-all simplicity would be a substantial advance. Recent literature still reports \(19/27\), approximately \(70.37\%\), as the RH-alone simplicity benchmark. [Literature discussion](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.02882)

Maybe the gradients smooth the singularity

**Your first instinct was right: \(L\) diverges.** The distinction is between differentiating \(\Delta\) and differentiating **\(\log\Delta\)**.

For two real roots separated by \(d\),
\[
\Delta=d^2,\qquad
\frac{d\Delta}{dd}=2d\longrightarrow0,
\]
so the determinant and its gradient are regular. But
\[
\frac{d}{dd}(-\log\Delta)=-\frac2d,
\qquad
\frac{d^2}{dd^2}(-\log\Delta)=\frac2{d^2}.
\]
The logarithmic derivatives amplify the singularity. Since \(L=\tfrac12\nabla^2(-\log\Delta)\), it contains precisely those inverse-square poles.

The exact heat example makes both your observations concrete:
\[
H(t,z)=z^2-2t,\qquad
\Delta(t)=8t,\qquad
\operatorname{spec}L(t)=\left\{0,\frac1{4t}\right\}.
\]
Here \(\Delta\) changes sign when the real pair becomes a nonreal conjugate pair. While all roots remain distinct and real, the **squared** Vandermonde stays positive.

That divergence is what the proposed detector uses. Multiplying by \(t\) gives a finite, nonzero collision signature; a bounded spectral filter also keeps each contribution finite. **Neither removes the evidence of multiplicity.**

So the almost-all strategy is to bound **how many eigenvalues become large**, allowing a sparse exceptional set—not to prove that \(L\) remains bounded through every collision.
